passage:
Dear Nirmala Didi,
You asked why I've been so quiet on our calls. It's a boy in Class 12 who's been taking the juniors' lunch money behind the gym and slapping anyone who says no. Last week he saw me watching and said, 'Say a word and you're next.'
I've been scared every single day. I wanted to tell Sir, but what if he found out it was me?
Then I remembered what you said about the anonymous box outside the counsellor's room. So on Tuesday I wrote down everything, the place, the times, the boy's name, and dropped it in without my name. I also told Amma, and she said I was right to be scared and right to report.
Now I walk to the bus with Kunal and his brother, never alone. Today the counsellor and the vice principal stood behind the gym all lunch. Nobody went near it.
I'm still nervous. But it feels like the grown-ups are carrying it now, not me.
Hrithik

qa.q: Where did Hrithik put the written report?
qa.a: In the anonymous box outside the counsellor's room, without a name.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling after the boy's warning?
qa.a: Hrithik felt scared every single day, afraid of being next if the report was traced.

qa.q: Which steps kept Hrithik safer while still reporting?
qa.a: Using the anonymous box, telling Amma, and walking to the bus with Kunal and his brother instead of alone.

qa.q: How might the juniors feel seeing adults behind the gym at lunch?
qa.a: Relieved and safer, since adults were now handling the danger.

grounding: A letter from a teen afraid of a bully's retaliation who uses an anonymous report, stays in a group and lets adults handle the danger.

passage: People think telling is easy. It isn't. I'm Arohi, and last year a girl in Class 11 decided I was her target. Pushing my tray, hissing things on the stairs, and once: 'If you go crying to anyone, I'll make it worse.' I believed her. For a month I said nothing. Then Sahil, my lab partner, noticed I was taking the long staircase every day and asked why. I told him, and he said, 'You don't have to put your name on it.' He was right. Our school has an online form where you can report without your name. I filled it in that night, with dates and places, while Mumma sat next to me. After that I made sure I was never alone on the stairs; Sahil and two others walked with me. Within a week the girl was called in with her parents. The teachers handled it. I never had to face her. Being scared was sensible. Staying silent wasn't.

qa.q: What did the girl say would happen if Arohi told anyone?
qa.a: 'If you go crying to anyone, I'll make it worse.'

qa.q: Why did Arohi stay silent for a month?
qa.a: Arohi felt frightened and believed the threat that things would get worse.

qa.q: What made reporting feel possible for Arohi?
qa.a: The school's anonymous online form, Mumma sitting alongside, and friends walking together on the stairs.

qa.q: How did Sahil notice something was wrong?
qa.a: He saw Arohi taking the long staircase every day and asked why, showing he was paying attention.

grounding: A spoken account of a teen afraid of a bully's retaliation who reports anonymously, stays with friends and lets teachers handle it.

passage: In Year 10 history in Bergen, Tomas read out his group's answer, then added in a slow, dragging voice, 'Like Emil would say it,' mimicking Emil's stammer. Half the class laughed. Emil stared at his desk. Freya's heart was thumping. She wasn't a speech-maker. She didn't stand up. She just said, clearly and not loudly, 'That's not funny, Tomas.' The laughter stopped as if someone had switched it off. Tomas rolled his eyes. 'Relax, it's a joke.' 'Not to him,' Freya said, and went back to her notes. Under the desk her hands were shaking. After class two classmates caught up with her. 'I wanted to say something too,' one admitted. The next week, when someone started a similar joke in the corridor, three people said 'Don't' at once. Freya noticed. Something had shifted.

qa.q: What did Freya say to Tomas?
qa.a: 'That's not funny, Tomas.'

qa.q: What was Freya feeling when she spoke up?
qa.a: She was nervous, her heart thumping and hands shaking, but determined to stay calm.

qa.q: What made Freya's stand effective?
qa.a: It was calm and short, not a speech, and it gave others the courage to speak up later.

qa.q: How might Emil have felt when Freya spoke up?
qa.a: Probably relieved and less alone, after staring at his desk while others laughed.

grounding: Shows a teen calmly speaking up in class against a humiliating joke, and how a small stand shifts what classmates accept.

passage: The coaching centre in Kota had a strict rule against phones in class, but Naveen had his out anyway, passing round a photo of Bittu asleep on his desk, mouth open. Someone had added a caption: 'Future topper 😴'. Bittu, who worked nights at his uncle's dhaba to pay the fees, was sitting two rows ahead, pretending not to hear. Ramesh felt his face go warm. He wasn't brave, not like in films. But when the phone reached him, he didn't pass it on. He put it face down and said quietly, 'He works nights to be here. Delete it.' Naveen snorted. 'You're no fun.' 'Maybe. Still delete it.' A couple of boys shifted awkwardly. Then one of them said, 'Yeah, man, delete it.' Naveen deleted it, grumbling. Bittu glanced back once. Ramesh just nodded. By the next week nobody was passing photos round in that class.

qa.q: Where does Bittu work at night?
qa.a: At his uncle's dhaba, to pay the fees.

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling when the phone reached him?
qa.a: His face went warm with nerves; he didn't feel brave, but he was uncomfortable with the cruelty.

qa.q: What did Ramesh's quiet approach get right?
qa.a: He stopped the photo spreading, gave a calm reason and stood firm without a scene, so others joined in.

qa.q: How might Bittu have felt when he glanced back?
qa.a: Probably grateful and a little less humiliated, seeing that someone had defended him.

grounding: Shows a teen quietly refusing to pass on a humiliating photo and asking for it to be deleted, and how that small stand changes the class norm.

passage: Afreen had forgotten about the canteen incident until Rafiq stopped her on the Andheri station staircase on Friday. The week before, when some boys mocked his lisp as he ordered samosas, she had simply said, 'Let him order,' and stood beside him until they drifted off. Now he held out a folded paper. 'I'm bad at saying things,' he said, not quite looking at her. 'So I wrote it.' The note said: 'Thank you for seeing me. Nobody's done that since I joined.' Afreen's first instinct was to wave it off: it was nothing, anyone would have. She stopped herself. 'Thank you for telling me,' she said instead, and tucked the note into her ID card cover. Rafiq smiled, relief all over his face. On the train home she read it again. She'd said three words. They had mattered more than she'd guessed.

qa.q: Where did Afreen keep Rafiq's note?
qa.a: In her ID card cover.

qa.q: How did Afreen feel reading the note on the train home?
qa.a: She felt moved and a little surprised that three words had mattered so much 😊

qa.q: Why was saying 'Thank you for telling me' better than waving it off?
qa.a: It accepted Rafiq's gratitude and honoured his effort to write it, instead of shrinking what he felt.

qa.q: What did Afreen's stand mean to Rafiq?
qa.a: It made him feel seen for the first time since he joined, which is why he wrote the note.

grounding: Shows a teen quietly thanked by a classmate she defended, choosing to accept it and realising being seen mattered to him.

passage:
'Darshan, wait up.' Eshaan jogged across the nets, bat under his arm.
'What's up?'
'Nothing. Just... that thing in the group chat. When they kept calling me "chipmunk" and you wrote "Enough, guys."'
'Oh. That was nothing.'
'It wasn't nothing.' Eshaan scuffed the ground. 'Everyone else sent laughing faces. You were the only one.'
Darshan opened his mouth to say anyone would've done it, then closed it. 'Okay,' he said. 'I'm glad it helped.'
'It did. My mum noticed I stopped hiding my phone at dinner.'
'Did they stop?'
'Mostly. Two of them even said sorry.'
'Good.' Darshan tapped his bat against Eshaan's pad. 'You can tell me if it starts again.'
'I know. That's kind of the point.' Eshaan grinned. 'Also, you owe me a net session. You got me out twice last week.'
'Deal. Tomorrow, six o'clock.'

qa.q: What did Darshan write in the group chat?
qa.a: 'Enough, guys.'

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling when Eshaan thanked him?
qa.a: He felt a little awkward and tempted to brush it off, then glad his words had helped.

qa.q: What did Darshan do right in this conversation?
qa.a: He accepted the thanks instead of dismissing it, and offered to be there if the teasing starts again.

qa.q: How did Darshan's message change things for Eshaan?
qa.a: Eshaan felt less alone and stopped hiding his phone at dinner, since one person had stood with him.

grounding: Shows a teen thanked quietly by a classmate he defended online, accepting the thanks and learning that being seen mattered.

passage: Monday. On the back stairs, Minakshi saw two seniors jostling Shalini, knocking her bag down, laughing. Minakshi pretended to check her phone and walked the other way. Not her business, she told herself. Thursday. Shalini came to school with her arm in a sling. She'd 'slipped' on the same stairs, she said. Minakshi felt sick all through maths. She knew what 'slipped' probably meant, and she had watched it start. That night she couldn't eat. The following Monday. Minakshi went to the class teacher before assembly and told her everything she had seen, with the day and the time. Ms Rao thanked her, spoke with Shalini and the counsellor that morning, and called in the seniors' parents. At lunch Minakshi found Shalini alone. 'I saw them last week and said nothing. I'm really sorry.' Shalini was quiet, then said, 'You said something now.' Next time, Minakshi promised herself, she would not wait.

qa.q: What was on Shalini's arm on Thursday?
qa.a: A sling.

qa.q: How did Minakshi feel after seeing Shalini's sling?
qa.a: She felt sick with guilt, knowing she had watched the pushing begin and said nothing.

qa.q: What did Minakshi do to act on her guilt?
qa.a: She told the class teacher exactly what she had seen and apologised to Shalini directly.

qa.q: How does Shalini seem to see Minakshi's apology?
qa.a: She is quiet at first, then acknowledges that Minakshi has spoken up now, which seems to matter to her.

grounding: Shows a teen who stayed silent before a classmate got hurt, feeling guilt, then reporting, apologising and resolving to speak sooner.

passage: Sahil, you asked why I made you promise to always speak up. Sit. When I was fourteen, in Shimla, a group of girls in my class kept daring my friend Tara to walk along the edge of the school's back wall. I knew it was dangerous. I watched three days in a row and said nothing, because the ringleader was the most popular girl in school. On the fourth day Tara slipped and broke her ankle. I cried all night. I thought I was the worst friend in the world. The next morning my father said, 'The guilt means your heart is working, Charu. Now use it.' I went to the headmistress and told her about the dares, and she stopped them that same day. Then I went to Tara's house and said sorry. She forgave me, slowly. That's why, Sahil. Speak up on the first day, not the fourth.

qa.q: What did the girls dare Tara to do?
qa.a: To walk along the edge of the school's back wall.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling the night Tara broke her ankle?
qa.a: Charu felt crushing guilt, crying all night, sure of being the worst friend in the world.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Charu's story?
qa.a: The father saying guilt means the heart is working, which led Charu to tell the headmistress and apologise to Tara.

qa.q: How did Tara respond to Charu's apology?
qa.a: She forgave Charu slowly, suggesting the hurt was real but the apology mattered.

grounding: An elder's story of staying silent before a friend got hurt, then using the guilt to report, apologise and resolve to speak sooner.

passage:
Dear Lavanya,
I'm writing this instead of saying it because I'd cry.
You know I forgot to upload our group project before the deadline. After Ma'am announced it in class, I went home and spent the whole evening calling myself names. Stupid. Useless. Can't be trusted with anything. I even wrote 'idiot' in the margin of my notebook, over and over.
Then I remembered last year, when you forgot your lines in the play. I told you, 'Everyone blanks. You're not your worst five minutes.' And I meant it.
So why is the voice in my head so much meaner to me than I'd ever be to you?
I tried talking to myself the way I talked to you. It felt fake at first. But then I actually made a plan: I emailed Ma'am to ask if we could submit late with a mark cut, and I set two phone reminders for next time.
Sorry I let the group down. I'm working on not being cruel to myself about it.
Hansa

qa.q: What did Hansa write in the margin of the notebook?
qa.a: 'Idiot', over and over.

qa.q: How was Hansa feeling that evening after the announcement?
qa.a: Hansa felt deeply ashamed and angry about the mistake, turning it into names like stupid and useless.

qa.q: What helped Hansa move from self-attack to action?
qa.a: Asking what would be said to Lavanya in the same spot, then emailing Ma'am and setting reminders.

qa.q: How might Lavanya feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Probably touched and ready to forgive, remembering Hansa's kindness when Lavanya forgot those lines in the play.

grounding: A letter from a teen who calls themself stupid after a mistake, notices the cruel voice, asks what they'd tell a friend and makes a plan.

passage: Santosh, you asked what's up with me lately. Okay. I'm your cousin Jatin, and last Saturday I reversed Papa's scooter into the neighbour's gate. Scratched both. Papa wasn't even that angry. But my head was. For three days it ran on repeat: you're so stupid, you ruin everything, you can't do one thing right. I didn't even want to go to football. Then on Tuesday Coach made me lead the drill, and when Aryan missed a pass I shouted, 'You're useless!' He looked so hurt. And I thought, wait. That's exactly what I've been saying to myself. I'd never let anyone talk to him like that. So why me? That night, when the voice started, I asked what I'd tell Aryan. It was: 'You messed up. Fix what you can. Practise.' So I apologised to Aryan, offered to help repaint the gate, and asked Papa to practise reversing with me on Sunday.

qa.q: What did Jatin reverse the scooter into?
qa.a: The neighbour's gate.

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling in the three days after the scooter accident?
qa.a: Jatin felt ashamed and full of self-contempt, with a cruel voice repeating 'you're so stupid'.

qa.q: What question helped Jatin quiet the cruel voice?
qa.a: Asking what would be said to Aryan, which led to apologising, helping repaint the gate and practising.

qa.q: How might Aryan have felt when Jatin shouted 'You're useless'?
qa.a: Hurt and small, which is what made Jatin notice the same cruelty inside.

grounding: A spoken account of a teen who attacks themself after a mistake, notices the cruel voice through hurting a teammate, and answers it with friend-like kindness.

passage: Aadhya was proofreading the final page of the school newspaper, forty minutes before the print run, when she saw it: she'd written that Kashish's cousin, not Kashish, had won the state essay prize. Her own mistake, in her own headline. Her stomach dropped. The old printer in the staffroom was already warming up, and the teacher in charge had gone to a meeting. For a moment she wanted to hide under the desk. Then she breathed and told herself, the way she'd tell a junior: 'Okay. It stings. You're allowed to feel that. Now fix it.' She messaged Kashish first: 'I got your name wrong in the headline. So sorry. Fixing it now.' Kashish replied, 'Thanks for catching it!' Aadhya corrected the page, printed a fresh proof and checked every other name twice. Then she added one line to the team checklist: 'Names checked by two people.' The paper went out on time.

qa.q: What mistake did Aadhya find in the headline?
qa.a: She'd written that Kashish's cousin, not Kashish, had won the state essay prize.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling when she spotted the error?
qa.a: Her stomach dropped with embarrassment, and for a moment she wanted to hide.

qa.q: How did Aadhya combine kindness with high standards?
qa.a: She let herself feel the sting without attacking herself, then apologised, fixed it, double-checked every name and added a checklist rule.

qa.q: How does Kashish see Aadhya's message?
qa.a: Kashish is grateful the mistake was caught and shared straight away.

grounding: Shows a teen who owns a mistake under deadline pressure, feels the sting and treats herself kindly enough to fix it well.

passage: At the inter-school relay in Chennai, Uma dropped the baton on the last exchange, and her team finished fourth instead of first. Walking back past the stands, she felt it burn: the gasp from the crowd, Mahima's face as she waited with her hand out for a baton that never came. On the bus, the old voice started: you always choke. Uma caught it. She thought of what she had said to Mahima last month after Mahima's false start: 'One bad exchange doesn't make you a bad runner. Let's drill it.' So she said it to herself, quietly. Then she turned round in her seat. 'Mahima, that was on me. I'm sorry. Can we practise exchanges every morning this week?' Mahima blinked, then grinned. 'Seven o'clock?' For five mornings they passed the baton until it felt like a handshake. At the zonal meet, the exchange was clean.

qa.q: Where did Uma's team finish in the relay?
qa.a: Fourth instead of first.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling walking back past the stands?
qa.a: She felt the burn of shame and disappointment, replaying the gasp and Mahima's face.

qa.q: How did Uma treat herself in a way that led to improvement?
qa.a: She talked to herself as she had to Mahima, owned the mistake, and set up daily exchange practice.

qa.q: How does Mahima respond to Uma's apology?
qa.a: She seems surprised, then happy to practise, suggesting she values the apology and the plan.

grounding: Shows a teen who acknowledges a costly mistake, feels the sting, and treats herself kindly while holding high standards to fix it.

passage: Irfan had knocked the class's only good microscope off the bench during the practical exam rehearsal, and the lens cracked in front of everyone. The teacher sighed that it would come out of the lab fund, and Irfan wanted to disappear. That evening a power cut left his lane in darkness, and he sat on the steps outside his building, phone dead, with nothing but the replay in his head. Clumsy. Useless. Gopika found him there, holding a torch and two cups of tea from her mother. 'Everyone messes up,' she said, sitting down. 'I once set the chemistry lab bin on fire. Small fire, but still.' He laughed despite himself. She stayed until the lights came back, talking about nothing. Climbing the stairs later, Irfan felt lighter, as if someone had lifted half of it off his back. The next week, when a junior spilled ink all over the notice board, Irfan was the one who said, 'Happens to everyone.'

qa.q: What did Gopika bring when she found Irfan?
qa.a: A torch and two cups of tea from her mother.

qa.q: How did Irfan feel climbing the stairs later?
qa.a: He felt lighter, as if someone had lifted half the weight off his back 🙂

qa.q: How did Irfan pass on what Gopika gave him?
qa.a: When a junior spilled ink on the notice board, he said, 'Happens to everyone.'

qa.q: How does Gopika see Irfan's mistake?
qa.a: As an ordinary slip anyone could make, like her own small fire in the chemistry lab.

grounding: Shows a teen weighed down by a public mistake whose friend says everyone messes up and stays, lifting the weight, which he then passes on.

passage: Vikas had typed a snarky comment about the class monitor, meant for his cousin, and sent it to the whole class group instead. He deleted it in seconds, but screenshots had already been taken. By lunch he had apologised to the monitor, who said a cold 'fine', and he was sitting on the back steps of the Lucknow school hating himself. Himani sat down next to him with her lunchbox. 'You look like you've committed a crime.' 'I'm the worst.' 'You said something mean and sent it to the wrong place. That's messing up, not being the worst. Everyone messes up. I once sent my crush's name to the family group.' He groaned into his hands, but he was half laughing. She stayed the whole lunch break. The weight in his chest eased. That evening he messaged the monitor again, a proper apology. And when his sister made a mistake the next week, he told her what Himani had told him.

qa.q: Where was Vikas sitting at lunch?
qa.a: On the back steps of the Lucknow school.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling before Himani sat down?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and full of self-hatred, calling himself the worst.

qa.q: What did Vikas do after Himani's support?
qa.a: He sent the monitor a proper apology and later passed Himani's words on to his sister.

qa.q: How does Himani see Vikas's mistake?
qa.a: As messing up, which everyone does, not as proof he is a bad person.

grounding: Shows a teen ashamed after a mean message went to the wrong group, whose friend stays and says everyone messes up, softening his self-judgement.

passage: Vandana Didi, you asked why I've been off all week. I'll tell you straight. I'm Omkar, and I lied to my parents. I said I was at Nikhil's for a project and actually went to a concert in the city till one in the morning. My phone died. When I got home, Aai was sitting on the stairs, eyes red, and Baba had been driving round looking for me. Aai didn't shout. She just said, 'I don't know who you are right now.' That hit harder than any shouting. For two days I felt like nothing, like I'd ruined everything. Then I thought: I did a terrible thing. That doesn't make me a terrible person. It means I have to fix it. So I apologised to both of them, properly, no excuses. I gave Baba my phone password and said, 'Check whenever you want. I want to earn it back.' Yesterday Aai made my favourite poha. Small step.

qa.q: What did Aai say when Omkar got home?
qa.a: 'I don't know who you are right now.'

qa.q: How did Omkar feel in the two days after the lie came out?
qa.a: Omkar felt worthless and ashamed, as if everything had been ruined.

qa.q: What steps did Omkar take to repair trust?
qa.a: Apologised to both parents without excuses, and offered Baba the phone password to earn trust back.

qa.q: How might Aai have felt sitting on the stairs that night?
qa.a: Terrified and hurt, not knowing where her child was, then betrayed by the lie.

grounding: A spoken account of a teen whose lie upset their parents, separating the act from the self, apologising and asking to earn back trust.

passage: Saturday night. Damini had borrowed Mummy's gold jhumkas for Parul's party without asking, and came home with only one. When Mummy saw the bare ear, her face went still. 'Those were my mother's,' she said, and walked away. Damini lay awake thinking, I'm the worst daughter, I ruin everything. Monday. She couldn't eat breakfast. Then she remembered what her aunt once said: you made a bad choice, you're not a bad person. So after school she went back to Parul's house and searched the whole terrace with Parul, on hands and knees. They found the jhumka behind a flowerpot. Wednesday. Damini put both earrings in Mummy's hand and said, 'I'm so sorry I took them without asking. I know I broke your trust. Can I show you I can earn it back?' Mummy held the jhumkas for a long time. Then she pulled Damini close. 'Ask me next time. And yes, you can.'

qa.q: Where did Damini and Parul find the jhumka?
qa.a: Behind a flowerpot on the terrace.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling as she lay awake on Saturday night?
qa.a: She felt worthless and ashamed, thinking she was the worst daughter.

qa.q: How did Damini repair the mistake?
qa.a: She searched with Parul, returned both earrings, apologised without excuses, and asked for a chance to earn back trust.

qa.q: Why was Mummy so upset about the jhumkas?
qa.a: They were her mother's, so losing one felt like losing a precious memory, and taking them without asking hurt her trust.

grounding: Shows a teen who feels worthless after upsetting her mother, separating the act from herself, repairing it and asking to earn trust again.

passage:
Thursday night. For almost two weeks everything has felt grey and pointless. I've been hating myself for everything: the maths test, the way I talk, even for being tired. Today in the library I wrote 'what's the point of me' in the back of my rough book, and Irfan saw it. He didn't laugh. He said, 'Come with me,' and walked me straight to Mrs Dsouza, the counsellor. I almost ran. But I told her. She listened, said I wasn't a burden, and said feelings like this can change with help. She called Ammi while I sat there, and Ammi came to school within the hour. Mrs Dsouza gave us a helpline number that's open all night and booked me in with a doctor tomorrow. Tonight Ammi sat on my bed till late and made me promise to wake her if it gets bad. I don't feel fixed. But I'm not carrying it alone any more.
- Rafiq

qa.q: What did Rafiq write in the back of the rough book?
qa.a: 'What's the point of me'.

qa.q: How had Rafiq been feeling for almost two weeks?
qa.a: Rafiq felt hopeless and full of self-hatred, with everything seeming grey and pointless.

qa.q: Why was going to Mrs Dsouza right away the wise step?
qa.a: Feelings like these need a trusted adult now; she involved Ammi, a helpline and a doctor the same day.

qa.q: How did Irfan respond when he saw what Rafiq wrote?
qa.a: He took it seriously, didn't laugh, and walked Rafiq straight to the counsellor 🤍

grounding: A diary of a teen feeling hopeless and self-hating for days, telling a counsellor the same day and getting family, helpline and doctor support.

passage:
Ritu: are you awake
Yusuf: yeah. what's up
Ritu: I don't know. everything feels pointless. I've hated myself all week. today I just stayed in bed
Yusuf: I'm really glad you told me. are you safe right now?
Ritu: I think so. I just don't see the point of anything
Yusuf: ok. this is too big for just us two. can you wake your mum now? I'll stay on chat
Ritu: she'll be upset
Yusuf: she'd be more upset not knowing. please. or I can ask my dad to call her
Ritu: ok. going
Ten minutes later:
Ritu: she's here. she hugged me. she called the helpline number from school and I talked to someone. they were kind
Ritu: mum's sleeping in my room tonight and we're seeing the counsellor tomorrow first thing
Yusuf: I'm so proud of you. message me anytime
Ritu: thank you for not letting me keep it in

qa.q: Who did Ritu wake after chatting with Yusuf?
qa.a: Ritu's mum.

qa.q: How was Ritu feeling when messaging Yusuf?
qa.a: Ritu felt hopeless and full of self-hatred, seeing no point in anything after a week of it.

qa.q: What did Yusuf do that was right?
qa.a: Yusuf asked if Ritu was safe, said it was too big to keep between friends, and pushed for waking Mum that night.

qa.q: How does Ritu's mum respond?
qa.a: She hugs Ritu, calls the helpline straight away, and stays close that night before the counsellor visit.

grounding: A night chat where a teen shares hopelessness and self-hatred, and a friend gets a parent and a helpline involved the same night.

passage:
Sunday. Got 94 in the physics test. Everyone in class was happy for me. I came home and redid the whole paper at my desk till two in the morning because of the six marks I lost, and cancelled football with Imran as punishment. That's what I do. Anything less than full marks and I sort of sentence myself. Imran knocked this morning and asked why I'd skipped football. I said I didn't deserve it. He sat on my bed and said, 'Bhai, you're doing to yourself what nobody else would dare to do to you.' That stuck. So today I tried something new. Instead of 'perfect', I wrote 'one percent better' on a sticky note. I looked at the six marks, found it was one formula I'd mixed up, practised that for twenty minutes, and stopped. Then I went to football. Felt weird. Felt good. Tomorrow, one more small thing.
- Farhan

qa.q: What did Farhan write on the sticky note?
qa.a: 'One percent better'.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel about scoring 94?
qa.a: He felt it wasn't good enough and was frustrated and harsh with himself over the six lost marks.

qa.q: What small step helped Farhan break the pattern?
qa.a: Fixing just the one formula for twenty minutes, then stopping and going to football.

qa.q: How does Imran see the way Farhan treats himself?
qa.a: As harsher than anyone else would dare to be, which worries him enough to speak up.

grounding: A diary of a teen who punishes himself for anything below full marks, trying small good-enough steps toward improvement instead.

passage:
Swati: did you submit the coding project?
Uday: no. deleted it
Swati: WHAT. it was due tonight
Uday: the animation lagged for half a second. it looked amateur
Swati: uday it was amazing. I saw it yesterday
